Frenchie and Kimiko's storyline this season is probably the worst television I've seen. Even "Who has a better story than Bran the Broken?" from Game of Thrones season 8 made more sense. Frenchie, Colin and Kimiko get so many scenes and the climax was just the conversation last episode in which they talk about their past and their trauma. First, Frenchie has to deal with his past for the third time, which is not only repetitive but just bad. He starts a sexual relationship with a victim from his past, which practically rots his character inside. Colin doesn't play a role at all after episode 4, but viewers are supposed to build an empathetic relationship with him within those four 4 episodes, which just doesn't work. Frenchie then goes to prison to atone for his actions. He could have been sent to prison with a much more interesting plot, but it doesn't matter at all. I had initially thought with the internment camps that Frenchie's prison sentence would now be linked to the main plot and that it would have some significance. I thought wrong. He simply gets out again with the help of Butcher. What a stupid thing to do! Frenchie is right back where he was at the end of last season. This is probably the stupidest plot I've ever seen. Kimiko starts therapy to deal with a trauma. Doesn't want to talk about it, stops doing it, kills Shining Light people and doesn't want to talk to Frenchie about her trauma. Then she complains that Frenchie won't talk to her about his third past coping bullshit. In episode 7, she finally finds the strength to do so. Was this really the best the writers could come up with to give the two characters something to do this season?! They could have come up with something shorter and instead put more plot into the other storylines or developed the main plot there faster. They should have just given the two of them a few scenes throughout the season where they have fun, where Kimiko tries to overcome her trauma from the past and Frenchie helps her, and they kiss and become a couple in the middle of the season, which would have made the finale that much more emotional. And then we have MM and his family. It starts with finding Todd because his daughter misses him and is fighting at school because of it. Being a good family father, as Butcher calls him, he of course doesn't talk to his daughter about it and ask why she did it, but goes looking for Todd. Unnecessary plot. A few episodes later and a few weeks later, we learn that the daughter got into a fight because she's against Supes. MM develops a stress disorder and experiences a panic attack because he's fighting Supes and considers withdrawing and being with his family. He doesn't do this, of course, because this storyline wasn't meant to develop the characters and change the team permanently, but because we need filler plot to stretch a story for one season over two seasons. But Hughie's plot with his mother and father was very important, because.... ehhhh. They put his father in the center and let him die. That can certainly work, but seeing Hughie, his father and Annie happy together at a lunch and then later having his father die with Annie by his side to provide comfort would be way too short. You practically remove Annie completely from Hughie's plot, she lets her boyfriend, who she's been with for a very long time now, go to the hospital alone where he meets his mother and of course Hughie gives his father indirectly Compound V because chaos and drama. And to top it off, Hughie is sexually abused by his childhood idol Tek Knight and the only consequence of that was 10 seconds at the end of episode six. And, of course, the trauma and coping with grief no longer play a role in episode 7. It was just a filler plot. And what kind of show would it be where the partners in a relationship give each other comfort when they're going through a hard time? And then we have the Starlight plot. I don't even know where to start because it's as chaotic as an essay written by ChatGPT 3.0. She's set up as Homelander's adversary and then against Firecracker. She's confronted with her past and can no longer use her powers because it's stressing her out. None of this is addressed, discussed in any way by the other characters on the team or her boyfriend. Annie and Hughie live so much in separate worlds that they do nothing for each other. Instead of Frenchie, Kimiko, MM and Hughie's father plot, I would have definitely preferred to see more scenes of Hughie trying to help Annie out of her predicament. I don't know if this Strong Women stereotype is completely overreaching and the writers are refusing to let a partner help his partner when they're miserable in a healthy romantic relationship, or if the writers are just incompetent, but I can't enjoy this at all. At the end of the sex scene in episode 7 with Annie I briefly thought: Okay, no clarifying conversation, no being there for each other, a bit out of character, but at least there still seems to be a closeness between them, but nope. She's not the real Annie, but a shapeshifter pretending to be Annie. Oddly enough, the shapeshifter has shown more emotional intimacy than real Annie has shown with Hughie this season. I guess they're really living completely next to each other now, so he doesn't even realize he's dealing with a shapeshifter and not Annie. The fact that he puts down some of the qualities he loves about Annie in the final episode feels even more stupid and ridiculous. Their relationship practically didn't exist before the shapeshifter showed up. The season was really only worth watching for Homelander, Ryan, Butcher and A-Train, as well as the core plot and social critique. The assassination attempt on the president has aged very well with the weekend event. I just think it's a bit of a shame that Ashley and Ryan didn't get another scene. Where is Ryan now? Where is Ashley? The only thing that can be subjectively criticized is the decision to make Butcher a complete tough guy. If Grace hadn't ruined everything, Ryan probably would have gone over to the other side of his own accord and Butcher's softer side would have won. But others in the comments said that this is comic Butcher completely losing himself in his hatred of Supes.

The last 5 minutes saved all the stupid shit from this season lol. I think it was a slow season with a lot of just setting stuff up for Season 5. The plot seemed to be more in service of that than trying to tell a tight story like the first two seasons. But generally I liked most of the characterizations in this season. Homelander was kinda all over the place, which somewhat does make sense but also just feels like they had an end-point they wanted him to be at and a bunch of different story beats and they just threw them into a hat and pieced together an arc, it wasn't cohesive imo. Messy and rushed at best, and same goes for his relationship with Ryan. Ryan's own arc seemed to be sidelined despite it being so important to everything. And then of course there's Annie. This episode proved that Erin Moriarty has some serious acting chops, so I think the real issue is the writing. Her characterization in particular, and also her relationship with Hughie, has been the worst part of this season I think, and honestly I think it's been pretty bad since S3. It seems to be a lot of just Kripke / the writers soapboxing on their 'hot takes' on gender norms (which are really just the current prevailing attitude towards gender norms among young people). For a show that has shown the ability to maturely portray complex topics and make even the most awful characters sympathetic, they certainly seem devoid of empathy for Hughie / the male issues portrayed on the show through him. In almost every situation within his relationship with Annie or even just any time there is some commentary on gender, the only perspective that seems to be getting 'pushed' is where Hughie is the bad guy and should have known better and done better. Even when he's obviously the victim. I get it, they're making the clear case that Annie is a flawed character and so we shouldn't take her behavior as the 'correct' position to have or what the writers endorse, but even so, the show seems to not really care about being empathetic and understanding to Hughie's struggles and men's issues like male rape victims and other toxic gender norms and expectations that negatively affect men. It's either played for laughs or just comes up to reinforce a point about men being the problem.

Just finished the episode and wanted to have some quick comments on it. There's a lot of good stuff in this episode, the pacing was actually great overall. Kimiko and Frenchie getting together really REALLY ruins a lot of their character development and character writing. It kind of steps on the importance of family and platonic intimate bonds thrusting both of them in another romantic relationship. Their relationship was defined as something far stronger than a romantic connection and it added to both of their characters. Wish we got more of the Gen V characters, they felt shoe horned in at the end there. The Ryan / Mallory plot was great. Mallory fucked up, but her fuck up makes narrative sense -- they were clearly running out of time and desperate. Ryan's response, also makes narrative sense. Good  consistent writing here. Ashley plot was lacking... Her last episode was supposed to lean us into more moral ambiguity on her character. I was hoping that the names she was giving Homelander would be faked or she would Schindler's List it. Yet she takes temp V in an act of self preservation. She's an interesting character, but we're falling back on old tropes with her. I think this season was a bit too narrow. For the audience to be against the virus, we need to see FAR more supes that aren't evil. The show could've done with expanding on the other teams outside of the Seven and how there actually *are* good supes --- this would make the virus plot more morally compelling. Anthony Starr really sells the show as a whole as Homelander. His decline to watch was great, though I worry that we're getting into Deus Ex Machina territory with Sage. "Smartest Person In The World" characters tend to be writing cop outs where all routes inevitably lead to it being in "her plan". Not a fan, personally. There was 0 way Neuman was surviving. In fact, it would be narratively AWFUL if she survived. She's a traitor to the country, was on board for genocide, and a mass murderer for no reason outside of selfish goals. Forgiveness is not for her, no. The writing table really needs to be adjusted. Hughie's character and the plots that befall him are a fucking mess. I feel I must be taking crazy pills to see all the enthusiastic responses to this season and especially the finale. What a mess. I'll start with the things I actually felt were meaningful: Grace's death (could have built up how she felt about Ryan through a scene earlier in the season with Butcher instead of her seeing him as a surrogate for her grandchildren, but whatever) Neuman's daughter going to the group home, despite everything her mom tried to do for her. That's about it. The rest of the finale seemed a disaster tonally and emotionally. Why is Starlight angry and jealous about Hughie having been fooled by a doppelganger? What does she expect from him? So annoying and stupid. I get that Butcher has "finally" gone rogue again, something that is undercut by the dull repetition of him constantly making his own moves behind the back of the rest of the boys, but how does he decide to only kill Neuman in that instance and not pose a threat to absolutely anyone else in the room? It seems like his decision to kill her serves only to complicate the plot at a moment that doesn't feel like anything's at stake. It would be one thing if he killed her when she were literally within eyesight of Homelander and were seconds away from popping his head. More to the head popping, how does Neuman not kill Butcher the instant that he wraps his tentacles around her? Almost everything having to do with Frenchie and Kimiko this entire season was a complete wash. They end the season after a kiss after 8 episodes of pointless subplots, contrivances, and handwringing by the writers, leaving them having accomplished little more between the end of season 3 til now. And they're both still alive. Could have upped the emotional stakes by finally putting one of them out of their misery. The Deep suggests they kill Ashley and Homelander doesn't sense that she's standing outside the room listening to everything they're saying? And then she successfully takes Compound V? Isn't it supposed to carry a risk of premature death if taken as an adult? They really should have closed her arc up also. After all of the metaphors for treating Sage like a slave and dismissing her, she still comes back to help Homelander, because of what, personal pride? Where's her own pride as a human being, nay, as a black woman? And the setup of her dropping her journal completely doesn't pay off. Starlight flying off was cringey, an extraordinary use of her power that seemingly never was demonstrated or mattered until right then. This is the worst season yet. I have more I want to say but I need more time to sit with the ending. In a distant way it feels like the boys are on the backfoot again, but I also have the distinct sense that Amazon wants to move season 2 of Gen V forward before making any really consequential changes to the plot. No one of importance is dead, no one's changed allegiances, Homelander controls the government but in a practical sense little has changed other than our heroes taken into custody, the impact of which is dulled by all of the poor choices that got us there.
